domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: During a routine newborn examination on day 2 of life, the large, flat, bluish-grey skin lesion shown is noted over the infant's sacrum and right buttock. The baby is active, feeding well, and moves all limbs symmetrically. What is the most appropriate advice to give the parents?
options: Reassure them that it is a benign congenital birthmark that fades spontaneously by early childhood and document it in the CHDR
Arrange an urgent coagulation profile and skeletal survey to exclude non-accidental trauma or an inherited bleeding disorder
Refer to paediatric dermatology for pulsed-dye laser therapy within the first 6 months to prevent permanent disfigurement
Request an urgent lumbosacral ultrasound and spinal MRI to exclude occult spinal dysraphism beneath the skin lesion
Schedule an excision biopsy under local anaesthesia because congenital dermal melanocytic lesions carry high melanoma risk
optionRationales: Correct: Mongolian blue spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis) are benign, harmless birthmarks that require no treatment, usually fade by 3–5 years of age, and should be recorded in the Child Health Development Record (CHDR) so they are not mistaken for bruising.

Incorrect: Unlike traumatic ecchymoses, these lesions are non-tender, flat, uniform slate-grey macules present from birth and do not evolve through bruise colour stages, so a non-accidental injury workup is unwarranted.
Incorrect: Laser therapy is unnecessary because congenital dermal melanocytosis almost always fades spontaneously during early childhood without scarring or cosmetic sequelae.

Incorrect: Isolated sacral Mongolian blue spots are epidermal/dermal pigment findings and are not midline neurocutaneous markers of occult spinal dysraphism such as a sacral dimple above the gluteal cleft, hairy tuft, or lipoma.
Incorrect: Congenital dermal melanocytosis carries no significant malignant potential and does not require biopsy or surgical excision.
clinicalPearl: Always document Mongolian blue spots in the Child Health Development Record (CHDR) at birth so their benign slate-grey appearance is not misinterpreted as non-accidental bruising later in infancy.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Mongolian blue spots are benign congenital skin lesions requiring parental reassurance, CHDR documentation, and no active treatment.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 21-day-old term infant is brought for persistent jaundice and dark urine that stains the nappy yellow, accompanied by the stool appearance shown. On examination, the liver is palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin. Which underlying condition requires urgent diagnostic confirmation and surgical intervention before 60 days of age?
options: Breast milk jaundice
Extrahepatic biliary atresia
Physiological neonatal jaundice
ABO haemolytic disease
Gilbert syndrome
optionRationales: Incorrect: Breast milk jaundice causes prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a thriving infant who passes normal yellow-pigmented stools and clear urine.

Correct: Pale clay-coloured (acholic) stools with dark urine and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia beyond 14–21 days indicate obstructive cholestasis; extrahepatic biliary atresia requires urgent Kasai portoenterostomy ideally before 60 days of life to preserve liver function.
Incorrect: Physiological jaundice is unconjugated, resolves by day 14 in term infants, and never produces acholic stools or bilirubinuria.
Incorrect: ABO incompatibility presents within the first 24–48 hours with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, anaemia, and pigmented stools rather than acholic cholestatic stools at 3 weeks.
Incorrect: Gilbert syndrome causes mild intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia due to reduced UGT1A1 activity, typically manifesting in adolescence with normal stool colour.
clinicalPearl: Any infant jaundiced beyond 14 days (term) or 21 days (preterm) needs split (conjugated vs unconjugated) bilirubin testing; pale acholic stools and dark urine are red flags for biliary atresia requiring Kasai surgery before 60 days.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Persistent neonatal jaundice with pale acholic stools indicates cholestasis and requires urgent split bilirubin and fasting abdominal ultrasound to exclude biliary atresia.

sourceStation.title: Acholic (Pale Clay-Coloured) Stools — Biliary Atresia

4.3 Name a clinical condition that could cause the above in infants.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Pale / clay-coloured (acholic) stools (indicating absent bile flow / obstructive cholestasis). (4.2) Investigations: Split serum bilirubin (conjugated vs unconjugated) (conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia > 20% or > 34 µmol/L) + Fasting abdominal Ultrasound (triangular cord sign, absent/small gallbladder) ± HIDA scan / Intraoperative cholangiogram + liver biopsy (gold standard). (4.3) Condition: Extrahepatic biliary atresia (requires Kasai portoenterostomy ideally before 60 days of life!).

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 10-day history of unremitting fever, lethargy, and the abdominal examination findings outlined on his skin. Which triad of diagnoses most plausibly accounts for this clinical presentation?
options: Intussusception, infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and Hirschsprung disease
Minimal change nephrotic syndrome, simple febrile convulsion, and bronchial asthma
Enteric fever, acute leukaemia, and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Acute appendicitis, Meckel diverticulum, and viral laryngotracheobronchitis
Congenital hypothyroidism, physiological jaundice, and coeliac disease
optionRationales: Incorrect: These are structural or obstructive gastrointestinal conditions of infancy that do not typically cause a 10-day febrile illness with combined hepatosplenomegaly.
Incorrect: None of these conditions classically produce prolonged 10-day pyrexia with both hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

Correct: Prolonged fever (>=7–10 days) with hepatosplenomegaly in a child requires considering systemic infections (such as enteric fever, malaria, leptospirosis, EBV), haematological malignancies (acute leukaemia/lymphoma), and autoimmune syndromes (systemic JIA).
Incorrect: Acute appendicitis and Meckel diverticulum present with focal abdominal pain or GI bleeding rather than organomegaly, and croup causes acute stridor.
Incorrect: These chronic endocrine, neonatal, and malabsorptive disorders do not account for acute-subacute 10-day fever accompanied by hepatosplenomegaly.
clinicalPearl: In a child with prolonged fever (>=7–10 days) and hepatosplenomegaly, systematically consider three broad categories: infections (typhoid, dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, EBV), malignancy (acute leukaemia), and systemic JIA.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Hepatosplenomegaly with prolonged fever warrants evaluation for enteric fever, leptospirosis, malaria, acute leukaemia, and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A single packet of standard WHO reduced-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) is dissolved in 1 litre of clean drinking water to rehydrate a child with acute watery diarrhoea. What are the exact sodium concentration and total osmolarity of the prepared solution?
options: Sodium 90 mmol/L and total osmolarity 311 mOsm/L
Sodium 45 mmol/L and total osmolarity 180 mOsm/L
Sodium 115 mmol/L and total osmolarity 290 mOsm/L
Sodium 75 mmol/L and total osmolarity 245 mOsm/L
Sodium 60 mmol/L and total osmolarity 210 mOsm/L
optionRationales: Incorrect: 90 mmol/L sodium and 311 mOsm/L reflect the older standard WHO ORS formulation, which was replaced because reduced-osmolarity ORS decreases stool output and vomiting.
Incorrect: A sodium concentration of 45 mmol/L and osmolarity of 180 mOsm/L are lower than the WHO reduced-osmolarity formulation and provide inadequate sodium replacement.
Incorrect: 115 mmol/L sodium exceeds WHO ORS levels and increases the risk of hypernatraemia in young children with non-cholera diarrhoea.

Correct: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (20.5 g total per 1 L: NaCl 2.6 g, anhydrous glucose 13.5 g, KCl 1.5 g, trisodium citrate dihydrate 2.9 g) yields Na+ 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, Cl- 65 mmol/L, K+ 20 mmol/L, citrate 10 mmol/L, and a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L.
Incorrect: Although closer to hypotonic paediatric maintenance fluids, standard WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS specifically contains 75 mmol/L sodium and 245 mOsm/L.
clinicalPearl: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L) contains equimolar 75 mmol/L sodium and 75 mmol/L glucose to drive intestinal SGLT1 co-transport, plus K+ (20 mmol/L) for hypokalaemia and citrate (10 mmol/L) to correct acidosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Per 1 L of water, WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS contains NaCl 2.6 g, glucose 13.5 g, KCl 1.5 g, and trisodium citrate 2.9 g (Na+ 75 mmol/L; total osmolarity 245 mOsm/L).

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A term newborn develops severe central cyanosis and tachypnoea 4 hours after birth that fails to improve significantly on 100% oxygen. His chest radiograph is shown. Which immediate pharmacological intervention should be commenced before transferring the infant to a cardiac intensive care unit?
options: Intravenous indomethacin (prostaglandin inhibitor) bolus
Intravenous propranolol (beta-adrenergic blocker) infusion
Intravenous frusemide (high-ceiling loop diuretic) bolus
Oral sildenafil (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor) suspension
Intravenous alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) infusion
optionRationales: Incorrect: Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and closes the ductus arteriosus, which would precipitously worsen hypoxaemia and cause circulatory collapse in duct-dependent TGA.

Incorrect: Beta-blockers like propranolol are used for hypercyanotic ('tet') spells in Tetralogy of Fallot (which shows a boot-shaped heart and oligaemic lungs), not for pre-transfer ductal maintenance in TGA.
Incorrect: Loop diuretics reduce preload and do not establish systemic-pulmonary blood mixing in neonatal TGA; ductal patency with PGE1 and correction of acidosis/hypoglycaemia are the priority.

Incorrect: Sildenafil reduces pulmonary vascular resistance in pulmonary hypertension, whereas immediate survival in cyanotic TGA relies on maintaining ductal patency with IV PGE1 and urgent Rashkind septostomy.

Correct: The radiograph shows the classic 'egg-on-a-string' silhouette (narrow superior mediastinal pedicle and enlarged globular heart with pulmonary plethora) of Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA); IV prostaglandin E1 maintains ductus arteriosus patency to enable mixing before Balloon Atrial Septostomy.
clinicalPearl: An 'egg-on-a-string' CXR in a cyanotic newborn indicates Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA): start IV prostaglandin E1 immediately (monitor closely for apnoea!), correct acidosis/hypoglycaemia, and arrange urgent Balloon Atrial Septostomy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Cyanotic CHD with an 'egg-on-a-side' heart silhouette (TGA) requires urgent IV prostaglandin E1 infusion to keep the ductus arteriosus patent prior to cardiac ICU transfer.

sourceStation.title: Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA) CXR & Pre-Transfer Care
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05) Newborn baby presented with cyanosis and difficulty in breathing, diagnosed to have Transposition of the Great Arteries (CXR given).
1) What is the main abnormality in the X-ray?
2) List two (2) measures you would do before transferring this baby to Cardiac ICU.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) CXR abnormality: 'Egg-on-a-string' cardiac silhouette (narrowed mediastinal vascular pedicle + oval/enlarged heart) with increased pulmonary plethora. (2) Pre-transfer stabilisation: (a) Start IV Prostaglandin E₁ (Alprostadil) infusion immediately to maintain ductus arteriosus patency (watch for apnoea!); (b) Correct acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia & arrange urgent Balloon Atrial Septostomy (Rashkind procedure) if restrictive PFO/ASD (avoid excessive high FiO₂ which can constrict PDA unless hyperoxaemia test).

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 4-year-old boy weighing 16 kg develops generalised urticaria, inspiratory stridor, and hypotension 10 minutes after a wasp sting. Using the medication ampoule shown, what are the correct immediate dose and administration route?
options: 0.16 mL (0.01 mL/kg) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
0.16 mL (0.01 mL/kg) undiluted via rapid intravenous bolus
1.6 mL (0.1 mL/kg) intramuscularly into the upper deltoid muscle
0.16 mL (0.01 mL/kg) subcutaneously into the posterior upper arm
1.6 mL (0.1 mL/kg) diluted in normal saline via oxygen nebuliser
optionRationales: Correct: For paediatric anaphylaxis, 1:1000 adrenaline (1 mg/mL) is administered immediately at 0.01 mg/kg (= 0.01 mL/kg, so 0.16 mL for a 16 kg child) via the intramuscular route into the mid-anterolateral thigh.

Incorrect: Undiluted 1:1000 intravenous bolus adrenaline carries a high risk of fatal arrhythmias and severe hypertension; IV adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest (1:10,000) or specialist-titrated infusions.

Incorrect: 0.1 mL/kg of 1:1000 equals a ten-fold overdose (1.6 mg in a 16 kg child, exceeding the adult maximum of 0.5 mg); additionally, the anterolateral thigh achieves faster peak absorption than the deltoid.
Incorrect: Subcutaneous injection results in slow, erratic absorption compared with intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis of the anterolateral thigh.
Incorrect: Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) treats severe viral croup stridor, not systemic anaphylactic shock where immediate IM adrenaline is life-saving.
clinicalPearl: Know the 3 paediatric routes of adrenaline 1:1000: (1) Anaphylaxis -> 0.01 mL/kg IM anterolateral thigh; (2) Severe croup -> 0.5 mL/kg (max 5 mL) nebulised; (3) Cardiac arrest -> dilute 10-fold to 1:10,000 and give 0.1 mL/kg IV/IO.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Initial anaphylaxis treatment in children is 0.01 mL/kg (0.01 mg/kg) of 1:1000 adrenaline injected intramuscularly into the mid-anterolateral thigh.

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 15-month-old child presents with severe muscle wasting, bilateral pitting pedal oedema, flaky-paint dermatosis, angular stomatitis, and hypothermia (35.2°C) after prolonged poor intake. Capillary blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L, and peripheral perfusion is adequate without shock. Which initial management plan is most appropriate?
options: Infuse rapid 20 mL/kg normal saline boluses over 30 minutes alongside high-protein F-100 catch-up formula
Warm the child, treat hypoglycaemia, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, and initiate cautious F-75 starter feeds
Administer intramuscular iron dextran immediately on admission to correct nutritional anaemia before feeding
Prescribe oral frusemide 2 mg/kg twice daily to mobilise bilateral pitting oedema rapidly
Keep the child nil-by-mouth for 48 hours while correcting electrolytes with concentrated IV potassium boluses
optionRationales: Incorrect: Rapid IV fluid boluses in oedematous SAM without decompensated shock precipitate fatal cardiac failure, and high-protein F-100 is reserved for the rehabilitation phase after oedema resolves.

Correct: During the WHO stabilisation phase of Severe Acute Malnutrition (kwashiorkor/oedematous SAM), priority goes to correcting hypothermia and hypoglycaemia (<3 mmol/L), giving empirical antibiotics, and starting low-protein, low-sodium F-75 formula orally or via NG tube.

Incorrect: Routine iron supplementation is withheld during the stabilisation phase of SAM because free iron promotes bacterial proliferation and oxidative stress; it is introduced only once appetite returns in rehabilitation.
Incorrect: Nutritional oedema resolves safely with cautious F-75 feeding and electrolyte correction; diuretics worsen intravascular depletion and hypokalaemia in SAM.
Incorrect: Early small, frequent enteral F-75 feeds prevent hypoglycaemia and restore gut integrity; concentrated IV potassium boluses are dangerous and unnecessary.
clinicalPearl: In WHO stabilisation of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): treat hypoglycaemia/hypothermia/infection first, feed cautiously with F-75 (not F-100), avoid diuretics and routine IV fluids unless in shock, and withhold iron until rehabilitation.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Kwashiorkor presents with oedema and flaky-paint dermatosis (often with perioral/nutritional lesions) and requires careful WHO stabilisation rather than aggressive IV volume loading or early iron.

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 7-year-old child (actual weight 25 kg; ideal body weight 20 kg) is monitored in the dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) critical phase as shown on the fluid chart. At the 20th hour of plasma leakage, haematocrit rises markedly and pulse pressure narrows despite crystalloid therapy. Which fluids are indicated during the first 6 hours of leakage versus this 20th-hour peak?
options: Half-strength 0.45% saline initially; IV albumin with frusemide bolus at hour 20
Routine Dextran-40 colloid initially; 5% dextrose in normal saline at hour 20
Isotonic 0.9% normal saline initially; colloid (Dextran-40 or 6% starch) at hour 20
Packed red blood cells initially; oral rehydration solution alone at hour 20
10% dextrose in water initially; hypertonic 3% saline bolus at hour 20
optionRationales: Incorrect: Hypotonic 0.45% saline does not stay intravascularly during capillary leakage and worsens third-spacing/hyponatraemia, while frusemide is contraindicated during active plasma leakage shock.

Incorrect: Colloids are reserved for peak leakage/shock unresponsive to crystalloids rather than routine initial therapy, and 5% dextrose in normal saline cannot rapidly correct hypovolaemic shock at hour 20.

Correct: Per Sri Lanka MoH Dengue guidelines, critical phase leakage starts with isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline), escalating to a colloid bolus (Dextran-40 or 6% hetastarch at 10 mL/kg/hr) at peak leakage if rising PCV or shock fails to respond to crystalloids (or blood transfusion if concealed bleeding occurs).

Incorrect: Blood transfusion is indicated for concealed or overt haemorrhage (suggested by a falling haematocrit with persistent shock), not routinely in the first 6 hours; severe 20th-hour leakage requires IV resuscitation.
Incorrect: Hypertonic dextrose solutions cause osmotic diuresis and worsen intravascular depletion, and 3% saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia rather than routine DHF leakage.
clinicalPearl: Sri Lanka MoH DHF 48-hour fluid quota = Maintenance (24h M) + 5% body weight (50 mL/kg) calculated on Ideal Body Weight (2,500 mL for IBW 20 kg here); begin with 0.9% NaCl and escalate to Dextran-40/hetastarch if rising PCV or shock persists.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Critical phase monitoring charts guide initial isotonic 0.9% saline infusion and escalation to Dextran-40 or 6% starch boluses during peak plasma leakage or shock.

sourceStation.title: Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DHF) Critical Phase Fluid Quota
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
15. A 7-year-old child (weight 25 kg) was admitted due to dengue haemorrhagic fever (critical phase); fluid balance chart shown.
15.1 Calculate the fluid quota which can be given to this child.
15.2 What are the types of fluid given at: (a) First 6 hours of leakage, (b) At 20th hour of leakage?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (15.1) 48-hour Critical Phase Fluid Quota (Sri Lanka MoH Dengue Guideline): Formula = Maintenance for 24h (M) + 5% of body weight (50 mL/kg). For 25 kg: M = `(100×10) + (50×10) + (20×5) = 1,600 mL` + 5% deficit (`50 × 25 = 1,250 mL`) = 2,850 mL over 48 hours (Note: If ideal body weight 20 kg is used on chart: `1,500 + 1,000 = 2,500 mL`). (15.2) Fluid types: First 6 hours of leakage: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% Normal Saline); At 20th hour (peak plasma leakage / rising PCV unresponsive to crystalloid or shock): Colloid solution (Dextran-40 or 6% Hetastarch) at 10 mL/kg/hr (or blood transfusion if concealed haemorrhage).

domain: 4.4 PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCIES, DENGUE (DHF) & RESUSCITATION (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 6-year-old boy develops the intensely pruritic skin lesions shown on his forearm 15 minutes after receiving oral amoxicillin. He now appears anxious and slightly hoarse. Which physical sign most urgently indicates life-threatening progression requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline?
options: Blanching palmar erythema
Basal fine end-inspiratory crepitations
Positive Nikolsky sign
Inspiratory stridor
Palpable tender splenomegaly
optionRationales: Incorrect: Palmar erythema reflects peripheral vasodilation or chronic liver disease and does not indicate impending airway compromise.
Incorrect: Basal crepitations suggest alveolar fluid or pneumonia rather than acute upper airway obstruction or anaphylactic bronchospasm (which produces expiratory wheeze).
Incorrect: Skin sloughing on lateral pressure (Nikolsky sign) occurs in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, not acute urticaria/anaphylaxis.
Correct: Inspiratory stridor (alongside hoarseness or tongue/lip angioedema) signifies acute upper airway and laryngeal oedema in anaphylaxis, demanding immediate IM 1:1000 adrenaline.
Incorrect: Splenomegaly is a feature of infection, haematological malignancy, or portal hypertension and has no role in identifying acute anaphylactic airway obstruction.
clinicalPearl: Never treat acute urticaria with an antihistamine alone before checking airway (inspiratory stridor, hoarse voice, swollen tongue/lips), breathing (wheeze), and circulation (hypotension/tachycardia) for anaphylaxis.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: When evaluating urticarial wheals, actively exclude life-threatening anaphylaxis by checking for inspiratory stridor, angioedema, wheeze, and hypotension.

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with mild periorbital puffiness and the dark-coloured urine shown in the bottle, 2 weeks after an episode of acute exudative pharyngitis. Which initial investigation is most appropriate to confirm the cause of his urine discolouration?
options: Immediate percutaneous renal biopsy under real-time ultrasound guidance
24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and free metanephrines
Intravenous urogram (IVU) with non-ionic iodinated contrast medium
Serum total immunoglobulin E (IgE) level and aeroallergen prick tests
Urine full report (UFR) and light microscopy for erythrocytes and casts
optionRationales: Incorrect: Renal biopsy is invasive and reserved for atypical presentations of APSGN (such as nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistently low C3 >8 weeks, or rapidly progressive renal impairment).
Incorrect: Urinary catecholamines evaluate phaeochromocytoma or neuroblastoma and play no role in evaluating post-infectious tea-coloured urine.
Incorrect: IVU exposes the child to radiation and nephrotoxic contrast during potential acute nephritis and is not the initial investigation for suspected glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect: Total IgE and skin prick testing evaluate atopic disease and do not investigate macroscopic haematuria.

Correct: A UFR and urine microscopy distinguish true glomerular haematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria—classically APSGN) from haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, or lower urinary tract infection before targeted bloods (ASOT, C3, RFT).
clinicalPearl: In a child presenting with smoky/tea-coloured urine, always start with a Urine Full Report (UFR) + microscopy to confirm RBCs/RBC casts before ordering ASOT, C3 complement, renal function tests, and renal ultrasound.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Tea-coloured macroscopic haematuria post-pharyngitis suggests acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; start with UFR/microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts.

(B) Initial investigation: Urine Full Report (UFR) / Urine microscopy (looking for dysmorphic RBCs & RBC casts + proteinuria; followed by ASOT, C3 complement, RFT, renal USS).

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought with red-brown urine, mild oliguria, hypertension (124/84 mmHg), and periorbital oedema 2 weeks after healing impetigo. Which urine full report (UFR) finding is most pathognomonic of a glomerular origin in this condition?
options: Red blood cell casts alongside dysmorphic erythrocytes and + to ++ proteinuria
Positive dipstick blood with zero red blood cells on high-power microscopy
Isolated calcium oxalate crystals with normal urinary protein and zero casts
Heavy leukocyte esterase and nitrite positivity with pure isomorphic RBCs
Massive ketonuria and +3 glycosuria without microscopic erythrocytes or casts
optionRationales: Correct: Red cell casts formed within renal tubules together with dysmorphic RBCs and modest proteinuria (+ to ++) are pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding, most commonly due to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN).
Incorrect: Positive dipstick blood without RBCs on microscopy indicates haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis) or myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) rather than glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect: Crystalluria with isomorphic RBCs and absent proteinuria or casts points toward urolithiasis rather than glomerular inflammation.
Incorrect: Nitrites, marked pyuria, and isomorphic RBCs suggest bacterial urinary tract infection rather than post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect: Glycosuria and ketonuria reflect uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and do not explain red-brown macroscopic haematuria.
clinicalPearl: Remember the classic UFR quartet of APSGN: numerous dysmorphic RBCs, pathognomonic red cell casts, mild-to-moderate proteinuria (+ to ++), and granular/cellular casts; serum C3 is typically transiently low.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs with + to ++ proteinuria on UFR confirm glomerular haematuria, classically caused by acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

sourceStation.title: Red Urine in a 5-Year-Old Boy — UFR & APSGN
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04. Red urine in a test tube that belonged to a 5-year-old boy.
Give 4 findings expected on UFR, and the most likely cause.  [Specimen photo omitted in 2013 archive files]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: 4 UFR findings: (1) Numerous red blood cells (dysmorphic RBCs); (2) Red cell casts (pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding); (3) Proteinuria (+ to ++); (4) Granular/cellular casts & occasional pus cells (brown/smoky turbid appearance). Most likely cause: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) (differential: UTI, nephrolithiasis, IgA nephropathy, HSP).

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A previously healthy 4-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of high fever, cough, tachypnoea, and bronchial breathing over the right lower zone. His chest radiograph is shown. What are the commonest bacterial aetiological agent and first-line oral drug of choice?
options: Mycoplasma pneumoniae and oral ciprofloxacin
Streptococcus pneumoniae and oral amoxicillin
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and oral cephalexin
Pneumocystis jirovecii and oral co-trimoxazole
Haemophilus influenzae type b and oral metronidazole
optionRationales: Incorrect: Mycoplasma pneumoniae typically causes atypical patchy interstitial infiltrates in school-aged children and is treated with macrolides (azithromycin/clarithromycin), whereas fluoroquinolones are avoided as first-line paediatric therapy.

Correct: The radiograph demonstrates dense right lower lobe consolidation (lobar pneumonia); Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial pathogen in children >1 month, and high-dose oral amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day) is first-line therapy.
Incorrect: Pseudomonas pneumonia mainly affects immunocompromised or cystic fibrosis patients and is completely resistant to first-generation cephalosporins such as cephalexin.

Incorrect: Pneumocystis causes diffuse bilateral perihilar interstitial pneumonia in severely immunocompromised infants (e.g., untreated HIV), not focal lobar consolidation in an immunocompetent 4-year-old.
Incorrect: Hib incidence fell dramatically with pentavalent vaccination, and metronidazole has no activity against aerobic respiratory cocci or bacilli.
clinicalPearl: Right lower lobe consolidation in a 4-year-old = Streptococcus pneumoniae until proven otherwise; treat community-acquired lobar pneumonia with high-dose oral amoxicillin (or IV benzylpenicillin/cefotaxime/co-amoxiclav if severe).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of paediatric lobar pneumonia; high-dose oral amoxicillin is the drug of choice for outpatient management.

sourceStation.title: Right Lower Lobe Lobar Pneumonia (4-Year-Old Child)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4. This is an X-ray of a 4-year-old child.
1. What is your diagnosis?
2. Name the commonest aetiological agent.
3. What is the DOC (drug of choice) for this condition?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Right lower lobe lobar pneumonia. (2) Commonest bacterium: Streptococcus pneumoniae. (3) Drug of choice: Oral Amoxicillin (high-dose 80–90 mg/kg/day in divided doses; IV Benzylpenicillin / Cefotaxime / Co-amoxiclav if severe/admitted).

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 9-year-old boy evaluated in the paediatric outpatient clinic for poor exercise tolerance demonstrates the bilateral nail-bed finding shown. Which pair of paediatric conditions is most strongly associated with this physical sign?
options: Minimal change nephrotic syndrome and nutritional iron deficiency anaemia
Acute viral bronchiolitis and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Cyanotic congenital heart disease and cystic fibrosis (bronchiectasis)
Vitamin D deficiency rickets and uncomplicated simple febrile seizures
Acute rheumatic chorea and primary nocturnal enuresis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Uncomplicated minimal change disease and iron deficiency anaemia cause pallor or oedema (and koilonychia in severe chronic iron deficiency), not digital clubbing.
Incorrect: Both are acute self-limiting illnesses and do not persist long enough to induce periosteal and nail-bed vascular proliferation causing clubbing.

Correct: Digital finger clubbing in children classically occurs in cyanotic congenital heart disease (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot), chronic suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, empyema), infective endocarditis, and chronic liver/inflammatory bowel disease.
Incorrect: Rickets produces widened wrists/ankles and rachitic rosary rather than finger clubbing, and febrile seizures have no digital signs.

Incorrect: Rheumatic chorea causes involuntary movement abnormalities, whereas clubbing points to chronic hypoxaemia, chronic suppuration, or hepatic/GI disease (and subacute infective endocarditis if fever is present).
clinicalPearl: When you spot finger clubbing in a child, examine specifically for central cyanosis/murmurs (cyanotic CHD), coarse crackles/sputum (bronchiectasis/CF), fever/new murmur (infective endocarditis), and chronic diarrhoea/stigmata of liver disease.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Paediatric digital clubbing is associated with cyanotic congenital heart disease, bronchiectasis/cystic fibrosis, lung abscess/empyema, infective endocarditis, IBD, and chronic liver disease.

sourceStation.title: Digital Finger Clubbing
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
13.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Feature: Finger clubbing. Paediatric causes: Cyanotic congenital heart disease (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot), Bronchiectasis / Cystic fibrosis, Empyema / lung abscess, Infective endocarditis, Inflammatory bowel disease / Chronic liver disease / Coeliac disease.

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 7-month-old formula-fed infant continues to pass watery, frothy green-yellow stools with perianal excoriation 10 days after acute viral gastroenteritis. Stool full report shows: red cells nil, pus cells 2–3/HPF, ova/cysts/amoeba nil, and reducing substances: orange. What are the diagnosis and appropriate therapeutic intervention?
options: Intestinal giardiasis; prescribe 7 days of oral metronidazole without altering milk
Acute bacillary dysentery; commence oral azithromycin alongside loperamide syrup
Infantile coeliac disease; initiate a strict lifelong gluten-free diet immediately
Secondary lactose intolerance; use lactose-free infant formula alongside ORS and zinc
Cow's milk protein anaphylaxis; inject intramuscular adrenaline and stop oral feeds
optionRationales: Incorrect: Stool microscopy is negative for Giardia trophozoites or cysts, and giardiasis causes foul-smelling steatorrhoea rather than positive stool reducing substances.
Incorrect: Absent faecal red cells and minimal pus cells (2–3/HPF) exclude invasive bacterial dysentery, and antimotility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in infants.

Incorrect: Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption and villous atrophy over months after gluten introduction and is not diagnosed acutely via orange stool reducing substances post-gastroenteritis.

Correct: Positive (orange) stool reducing substances with acidic watery stools following gastroenteritis confirm transient secondary lactase deficiency; manage with temporary lactose-free formula for 2–4 weeks (breastfed infants continue breastfeeding) plus ORS and zinc.
Incorrect: Anaphylaxis causes acute airway, respiratory, or circulatory compromise within minutes of exposure rather than isolated post-infectious carbohydrate malabsorption.
clinicalPearl: Orange/brick-red stool reducing substances (Clinitest) post-gastroenteritis indicate secondary lactose intolerance from brush-border lactase loss; temporarily use lactose-free formula for 2–4 weeks in formula-fed infants, but NEVER stop breastfeeding.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Maintain hydration with ORS and zinc while addressing carbohydrate malabsorption (secondary lactase deficiency) with temporary lactose-free formula in formula-fed infants.

sourceStation.title: Lactose Intolerance (Stool Reducing Substances Positive)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

Amoeba / Giardia / Whipworm / Hookworm / Other organisms: Nil
Reducing substances: Orange

19.2 List two (02) therapeutic interventions indicated for this child.  [Text-only stool report station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (19.1) Lactose intolerance (secondary lactase deficiency, e.g., post-viral gastroenteritis). (19.2) Therapeutic interventions: (1) Temporary switch to lactose-free infant formula (or soy/lactose-free milk in older children for 2–4 weeks; continue breastfeeding if breastfed); (2) Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORS) + Zinc supplementation and avoid sugary/dairy-heavy drinks while maintaining adequate calorie nutrition.

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 2-year-old girl presents with delayed walking, bone pain, frontal bossing, and palpable beading at the costochondral junctions. Her right wrist radiograph is shown. Which pair of radiographic abnormalities confirms the diagnosis?
options: Dense white metaphyseal Frankel lines with subperiosteal haematoma calcification
Multiple punched-out lytic diaphyseal lesions with Codman triangle periosteal reaction
Premature closure of the distal radial physis with marked cortical hyperostosis
Diffuse osteosclerosis of the carpal bones with Erlenmeyer flask metaphyseal flaring
Cupping and fraying of the distal metaphyses with widening of the epiphyseal growth plate
optionRationales: Incorrect: A dense metaphyseal white line (Frankel line), Wimberger ring sign, and subperiosteal haemorrhage are classic radiographic features of scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), not rickets.
Incorrect: Aggressive lytic bone destruction with Codman triangle suggests osteomyelitis or malignant bone tumour (such as osteosarcoma/Ewing sarcoma) rather than metabolic bone disease.
Incorrect: Rickets causes delayed mineralisation and growth plate widening, not premature physeal fusion or cortical thickening.
Incorrect: Diffuse bone sclerosis ('bone-within-bone') and Erlenmeyer flask deformity characterise osteopetrosis or Gaucher disease rather than vitamin D deficiency rickets.

Correct: Unmineralised osteoid accumulation in rickets widens the radiolucent growth plate and causes flaring, cupping, and indistinct irregular fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses alongside generalised osteopenia.
clinicalPearl: Classic wrist X-ray triad in rickets: metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and splaying/widening of the growth plate; check serum Ca, low PO4, markedly elevated ALP, elevated PTH, and low 25(OH) vitamin D.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Wrist radiographs in rickets show cupping and fraying of the distal metaphyses, widening of the epiphyseal plate, and generalised osteopenia.

sourceStation.title: Rickets — Wrist X-Ray & Clinical Findings
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 02

2.2 Identify the condition. (2 marks)

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) X-ray findings: Cupping and fraying of metaphyses (indistinct irregular metaphyseal margins) and widening/splaying of the epiphyseal growth plate (plus generalised osteopenia). (2.2) Condition: Rickets (Vitamin D deficiency). (2.3) Clinical findings: Widened wrists and ankles, Rachitic rosary (beading at costochondral junctions), Harrison sulcus, Bowing of legs (genu varum/valgum), Frontal bossing, Craniotabes.

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 10-year-old boy with a BMI of 15 kg/m² presents with acute-onset secondary bedwetting, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss. His urine full report shows glucose +2, protein nil, red cells 3/HPF, and pus cells 4/HPF. After urgently screening for diabetic ketoacidosis, what is the definitive long-term treatment?
options: Lifelong subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin therapy with structured glucose monitoring
Oral metformin monotherapy titrated gradually against fasting blood glucose readings
Oral glibenclamide sulphonylurea twice daily alongside a strict sugar-free diet
Oral desmopressin at bedtime combined with strict evening fluid restriction after 6 pm
A 7-day course of oral cephalexin followed by a repeat urine culture in 2 weeks
optionRationales: Correct: New-onset nocturnal enuresis, weight loss, and +2 glycosuria in a lean 10-year-old indicate Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM); after excluding DKA with capillary glucose, ketones, and VBG, definitive management requires lifelong subcutaneous insulin.

Incorrect: Metformin is first-line for paediatric Type 2 diabetes (typically obese adolescents with acanthosis nigricans), whereas T1DM causes absolute insulin deficiency and risks fatal DKA without exogenous insulin.
Incorrect: Sulphonylureas require endogenous pancreatic beta-cell function and are ineffective in autoimmune Type 1 diabetes mellitus.
Incorrect: Desmopressin treats primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis; restricting fluids in a polyuric diabetic child precipitates severe dehydration and ketoacidosis.
Incorrect: The UFR shows negligible pus cells (4/HPF) and no nitrites, ruling out UTI as the primary diagnosis; glycosuria demands urgent diabetes assessment.
clinicalPearl: Secondary nocturnal enuresis + weight loss + glycosuria in a child is Type 1 diabetes mellitus until proven otherwise; always check capillary glucose, blood/urine ketones, and venous blood gas immediately to rule out DKA.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Assessment of Dehydration in Children OSCE Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Paediatric diabetes presenting with polyuria/enuresis and glycosuria requires immediate DKA screening (glucose, ketones, VBG; BSPED protocol if acidotic) and lifelong subcutaneous insulin.

sourceStation.title: Paediatric Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
12. 10-year-old boy presents with acute-onset bedwetting, BMI 15 kg/m².
Urine Full Report: Glucose +2 | Red cell 3 | Pus cell 4 | Colour: Pale yellow | Protein: Nil
12.1 What is the most likely diagnosis?
12.2 What is the definitive treatment?  [Text-only UFR station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (12.1) Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) (screen urgently for DKA with capillary blood glucose, blood/urine ketones, and venous blood gas). (12.2) Definitive treatment: Lifelong subcutaneous Insulin therapy (basal-bolus regimen) + structured diabetes education, SMBG/dietary carbohydrate management, and sick-day rules.

domain: 4.5 PAEDIATRIC RESPIRATORY, CARDIOLOGY, ENDOCRINOLOGY & GI (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of high fever, cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. His chest radiograph is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate initial management?
options: Bronchogenic carcinoma; arrange immediate CT-guided percutaneous core needle biopsy
Round pneumonia; start oral antibiotics and repeat the chest radiograph in 4–6 weeks
Pulmonary hydatid cyst; refer immediately for surgical thoracotomy and enucleation
Posterior mediastinal neuroblastoma; begin emergency multi-agent chemotherapy
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation; schedule urgent lobectomy before starting antimicrobials
optionRationales: Incorrect: Primary lung carcinoma is exceedingly rare in 5-year-olds, and invasive biopsy is inappropriate before treating and following up an acute febrile round consolidation.

Correct: Children <8 years have underdeveloped collateral ventilation (pores of Kohn and canals of Lambert), causing Streptococcus pneumoniae consolidation to appear as a well-defined round opacity with air bronchograms ('round pneumonia') that resolves with standard antibiotic therapy.
Incorrect: A hydatid cyst does not typically present acutely with a 2-day high fever and air bronchograms, and surgery is not indicated for uncomplicated bacterial round pneumonia.
Incorrect: Neuroblastoma is an extrapulmonary posterior mediastinal mass often causing vertebral/rib erosion or calcification rather than an acute febrile parenchymal opacity with air bronchograms.
Incorrect: Even if an underlying congenital cyst were suspected, acute febrile infection is treated first with antibiotics and reassessed by follow-up imaging at 4–6 weeks.
clinicalPearl: Round pneumonia is a classic paediatric mimic of a lung mass in children <8 years due to immature pores of Kohn and canals of Lambert; always treat fever + round opacity with antibiotics and confirm clearance on CXR in 4–6 weeks.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Well-circumscribed round parenchymal opacity with air bronchograms in a febrile child <8 years is round pneumonia (usually S. pneumoniae), managed with antibiotics and a 4–6 week follow-up CXR.

sourceStation.title: Round Pneumonia on Chest X-Ray (5-Year-Old)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01. This is an X-ray of a 5-year-old child.
1. What are the two abnormalities seen in this X-ray?
2. What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Abnormalities: Well-defined round/oval parenchymal opacity in the lung field (often posterior/lower lobe) with air bronchograms and absence of pleural effusion/bony rib erosion. (2) Diagnosis: Round pneumonia (classic in children < 8 years due to underdeveloped pores of Kohn & canals of Lambert; commonest organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae — treat with antibiotics and repeat CXR in 4–6 weeks to confirm resolution).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 5-year-old boy with difficulty climbing stairs and prominent calf enlargement is asked to stand up from the floor, demonstrating the sequence illustrated. Which physical sign is shown, and which initial blood test should be ordered first?
options: Positive Trendelenburg sign; serum alkaline phosphatase
Positive Babinski sign; serum caeruloplasmin
Positive Gower's sign; serum creatine kinase (CK)
Positive Romberg sign; serum vitamin B12
Positive Chvostek sign; serum parathyroid hormone
optionRationales: Incorrect: Trendelenburg sign evaluates hip abductor weakness on single-leg stance (e.g., developmental hip dysplasia), and alkaline phosphatase screens for metabolic bone disease rather than myopathy.
Incorrect: An extensor plantar response indicates an upper motor neurone lesion, and caeruloplasmin screens for Wilson disease.

Correct: Rising from the floor by pushing into a quadruped stance and 'walking' the hands up the thighs (Gower's sign) demonstrates proximal pelvic-girdle weakness typical of Duchenne muscular dystrophy; serum CK is markedly elevated (often >10,000 U/L) as the initial screening test.
Incorrect: Romberg sign assesses dorsal column proprioceptive ataxia while standing, not proximal muscle weakness rising from the floor.
Incorrect: Chvostek sign reflects facial nerve hyperexcitability in hypocalcaemia, not pelvic-girdle myopathy.
clinicalPearl: Positive Gower's sign + calf pseudohypertrophy in a young boy = Duchenne muscular dystrophy until excluded; order serum creatine kinase (CK) first (usually 10–100× normal) before dystrophin genetic testing.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Gower's sign reflects proximal pelvic-girdle weakness in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, screened initially with markedly elevated serum creatine kinase.

sourceStation.title: Gower's Sign & Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Q.3
A.) What is the sign shown?
B.) What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) Positive Gower's sign (proximal pelvic-girdle / hip extensor muscle weakness). (B) Diagnosis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) (X-linked recessive dystrophin deficiency; associated with calf pseudohypertrophy & markedly elevated serum CK).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 6-week-old infant delivered vaginally after difficult shoulder dystocia exhibits the resting posture of the right upper limb shown in the photograph. Which nerve roots are injured?
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1 nerve roots)
Isolated radial nerve at the humeral spiral groove
Isolated ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6 nerve roots)
Thoracic spinal cord segments T4–T6
optionRationales: Incorrect: C8–T1 injury (Klumpke palsy) causes intrinsic hand muscle paralysis ('claw hand') and often ipsilateral Horner syndrome, sparing shoulder abduction and elbow extension.
Incorrect: Isolated radial nerve palsy causes wrist and finger drop while preserving shoulder external rotation and biceps elbow flexion.
Incorrect: Ulnar nerve injury affects medial forearm and intrinsic hand muscles (ulnar claw) without causing shoulder adduction and internal rotation.

Correct: Lateral traction separating the head from the shoulder during shoulder dystocia stretches the C5–C6 roots (Erb-Duchenne palsy), paralysing the abductors/external rotators of the shoulder, elbow flexors, and supinators to create the 'waiter's tip' posture.
Incorrect: Mid-thoracic spinal injury spares the brachial plexus and causes lower-limb paraplegia rather than an upper-limb waiter's tip posture.
clinicalPearl: Erb's palsy (C5–C6) = 'waiter's tip' (arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated) with absent Moro/biceps reflex but intact palmar grasp; compare with Klumpke palsy (C8–T1) = claw hand + absent grasp + Horner syndrome.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Erb's paralysis results from C5–C6 brachial plexus traction injury during shoulder dystocia or breech delivery, producing the classic 'waiter's tip' arm posture.

sourceStation.title: Erb's Paralysis (C5–C6 Brachial Plexus Injury)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Photograph of an infant (right arm adducted, internally rotated, forearm extended and pronated — Erb's paralysis).
What is the diagnosis and most likely cause for this abnormality?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Diagnosis: Erb's palsy (Erb-Duchenne paralysis) — injury to C5–C6 roots (upper trunk of brachial plexus). Cause: Difficult vaginal delivery / shoulder dystocia causing excessive lateral traction separating head/neck from shoulder (macrosomia, breech).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: The bedside apparatus shown is used with centrifuged capillary tubes across paediatric wards in Sri Lanka. Which parameter does it measure, and what percentage change from baseline defines significant haemoconcentration in dengue haemorrhagic fever?
options: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR); a fall of 50% below baseline
Reticulocyte production index; a rise above 5% of total red blood cells
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration; a fall below 28 g/dL
Plasma colloid oncotic pressure; a fall below 15 mmHg
Packed cell volume (haematocrit); a rise of 20% or more above baseline
optionRationales: Incorrect: ESR is measured vertically in a Westergren tube over 1 hour and is not a bedside indicator of acute dengue plasma leakage.
Incorrect: Reticulocyte counts assess marrow erythropoiesis via supravital staining and cannot be read on a microhaematocrit scale.
Incorrect: MCHC is a red-cell index calculated on an automated haematology analyser rather than a capillary-tube microhaematocrit reader.
Incorrect: Although hypoalbuminaemia reduces oncotic pressure in dengue plasma leakage, a capillary-tube reader specifically measures cellular packed volume (PCV).

Correct: A Hawksley microhaematocrit reader measures Packed Cell Volume (PCV / haematocrit) from a spun heparinised capillary tube; in DHF, a >=20% rise above baseline indicates significant plasma leakage and haemoconcentration.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan dengue wards, bedside microhaematocrit (PCV) is checked 3-hourly during the critical phase; a >=20% rise above baseline (or >20% drop on recovery) confirms plasma leakage.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Packed Cell Volume (PCV) monitoring via capillary tube detects dengue plasma leakage, defined by a >=20% rise in haematocrit above baseline.

sourceStation.title: Packed Cell Volume (PCV / Haematocrit) Capillary Tube
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

2. Name 2 clinical situations where you do this test.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Packed Cell Volume (PCV / Haematocrit). (2) Clinical situations: Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DHF) (monitoring haemoconcentration / plasma leakage — ≥ 20% rise above baseline) and Polycythaemia / Severe dehydration / Anaemia.

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: An 11-month-old infant exclusively fed unfortified cow's milk with minimal weaning solids has pallor. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, MCV 67 fL, normal WBC, and normal platelets, with the peripheral blood film shown. Which pair of investigations should be ordered next to differentiate the two most likely diagnoses?
options: Serum ferritin (iron studies) and haemoglobin HPLC / electrophoresis
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test and bone marrow trephine biopsy
Serum vitamin B12, red-cell folate, and intrinsic factor antibodies
Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and D-dimer
G6PD enzyme activity assay and osmotic fragility testing
optionRationales: Correct: Marked microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 67 fL) with target cells and poikilocytosis at 11 months requires differentiating iron deficiency anaemia (low ferritin, elevated TIBC) from thalassaemia trait/intermedia/major (Hb HPLC/electrophoresis and parental FBC/HPLC).

Incorrect: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia with normal WBC and platelets does not suggest autoimmune haemolysis (normocytic/macrocytic reticulocytosis) or marrow failure requiring immediate trephine biopsy.
Incorrect: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies produce macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia (high MCV), not microcytic hypochromic anaemia with MCV 67 fL.
Incorrect: Coagulation studies investigate bleeding disorders or DIC and do not distinguish iron deficiency from thalassaemia syndromes.
Incorrect: G6PD deficiency causes acute episodic normocytic oxidative haemolysis, and osmotic fragility tests for hereditary spherocytosis (normocytic/hyperchromic spherocytes).
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lanka, always evaluate microcytic hypochromic anaemia in late infancy for BOTH iron deficiency anaemia (excess cow's milk, poor weaning) and thalassaemia (serum ferritin + Hb HPLC + parental indices).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia in an infant (low Hb and low MCV) warrants serum ferritin/iron studies and haemoglobin HPLC to distinguish iron deficiency from thalassaemia.

sourceStation.title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anaemia in 11-Month-Old
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5) Regarding the following investigations & blood film of an 11-month-old baby:
• Haemoglobin 8.5 g/dL  • MCV 67 fL  • WBC normal  • Platelets normal
a) What are the differential diagnoses for the above patient?
b) What are the further investigations?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Differential diagnoses: Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest at 9–12m) and Thalassaemia (trait or intermedia/major) (also lead poisoning/chronic disease). (b) Further investigations: Serum ferritin, serum iron & TIBC (iron studies) + Haemoglobin HPLC / Electrophoresis (and parental FBC/HPLC).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with mildly pruritic perioral skin lesions that developed over 4 days as shown in the photograph. Which pair of organisms most commonly causes this superficial skin infection?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis
Herpes simplex virus and Varicella zoster virus
Trichophyton rubrum and Microsporum canis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Gram-negative bacilli cause ecthyma gangrenosum or nosocomial wound infections in immunocompromised patients rather than childhood community impetigo.

Correct: Non-bullous impetigo presents with characteristic perioral honey-coloured crusts over erythematous erosions and is caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).
Incorrect: These respiratory colonisers cause acute otitis media and sinusitis rather than superficial crusted perioral skin lesions.

Incorrect: Viral vesicles cause painful punched-out ulcers or disseminated pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base ('dewdrop on a rose petal') rather than classic honey-coloured bacterial impetigo crusts.
Incorrect: Dermatophytes produce annular scaly plaques with central clearing (tinea faciei/corporis) or boggy scalp kerion rather than perioral golden crusts.
clinicalPearl: Perioral honey-coloured crusts = non-bullous impetigo (Staphylococcus aureus & Group A Strep); treat localised disease with topical mupirocin/fusidic acid or widespread disease with oral flucloxacillin/erythromycin.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Honey-crusted impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) and often complicates pre-existing eczema or minor trauma.

sourceStation.title: Impetigo (Non-Bullous Honey-Crusted)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
12. This is a photograph of a 2-year-old boy.
12.1 Name the clinical condition shown on this picture.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (12.1) Impetigo. (12.2) Causative organisms: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 2-year-old child presents with a 1-day history of intense itching and the generalised skin lesions shown. He is alert, afebrile, with clear chest auscultation, no stridor, no lip swelling, and normal vital signs. What are the diagnosis and appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Toxic epidermal necrolysis; immediate intravenous immunoglobulin and ICU care
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; intravenous flucloxacillin and barrier nursing
Acute urticaria; oral non-sedating H1-antihistamine (such as cetirizine)
Erythema multiforme minor; oral aciclovir and potent topical clobetasol
Infantile scabies; whole-body 5% permethrin cream left overnight
optionRationales: Incorrect: TEN presents with painful dusky skin, mucosal sloughing, and positive Nikolsky sign rather than pruritic migratory oedematous wheals.
Incorrect: SSSS causes diffuse tender erythema, flaccid bullae, and desquamation in infants/toddlers without pruritic wheals.

Correct: Transient, well-circumscribed erythematous oedematous wheals with surrounding flare in a systemically stable child indicate acute urticaria, managed first-line with an oral H1-antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine).
Incorrect: Erythema multiforme displays fixed symmetrical 'target' lesions with central dusky/vesicular zones rather than transient evanescent wheals.
Incorrect: Scabies causes persistent burrows, papules, and nocturnal pruritus over wrists/palms/soles rather than acute migratory urticarial plaques.
clinicalPearl: In a child with acute urticarial wheals, first exclude anaphylaxis (stridor, wheeze, hypotension); if absent, prescribe an oral non-sedating H1-antihistamine (cetirizine) and educate parents on warning signs.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute urticaria presents as transient erythematous oedematous wheals with flare and is treated with oral H1-antihistamines once anaphylaxis signs are excluded.

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 4-year-old boy demonstrates the floor-rising sequence captured in the 4-frame video storyboard and is diagnosed with the commonest inherited paediatric muscular dystrophy. What are the inheritance pattern and affected structural protein?
options: Autosomal recessive inheritance affecting survival motor neurone (SMN1) protein
Autosomal dominant inheritance affecting fibrillin-1
X-linked dominant inheritance affecting PHEX endopeptidase
X-linked recessive inheritance affecting dystrophin
Maternal mitochondrial inheritance affecting respiratory chain complex I
optionRationales: Incorrect: SMN1 deficiency causes autosomal recessive Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), characterised by diffuse lower motor neurone hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, and areflexia rather than DMD calf pseudohypertrophy.
Incorrect: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause autosomal dominant Marfan syndrome (tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation), not progressive pelvic-girdle muscular dystrophy.
Incorrect: X-linked dominant PHEX mutations cause vitamin D-resistant hypophosphataemic rickets, not muscular dystrophy.

Correct: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) follows X-linked recessive inheritance (Xp21 dystrophin gene mutation), causing absent dystrophin, progressive proximal weakness (Gower's sign), calf pseudohypertrophy, and late dilated cardiomyopathy/respiratory failure.
Incorrect: Mitochondrial disorders (e.g., MELAS, MERRF) show maternal transmission with multisystem lactic acidosis/encephalomyopathy rather than Xp21 dystrophin loss.
clinicalPearl: Both Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are X-linked recessive dystrophinopathies on Xp21 (Duchenne = absent dystrophin, onset <5 years; Becker = partially functional dystrophin, milder/later onset).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive myopathy caused by dystrophin deficiency, manifesting clinically with Gower's sign.

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with colicky abdominal pain, microscopic haematuria, normal platelet count, and the symmetrical rash shown over his buttocks and lower limbs. Which additional feature completes the classic clinical tetrad of this condition?
options: Destructive symmetrical small-joint deformities of the proximal interphalangeal joints
Desquamating strawberry tongue with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis
Sydenham chorea with migrating erythema marginatum over the trunk
Ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness with absent deep tendon reflexes
Symmetrical arthralgia or transient non-erosive arthritis of the knees and ankles
optionRationales: Incorrect: HSP arthritis is transient, oligoarticular, and strictly non-erosive, unlike rheumatoid-factor-positive polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Incorrect: Strawberry tongue, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, and cervical lymphadenopathy characterise Kawasaki disease rather than IgA vasculitis.
Incorrect: Chorea and erythema marginatum are Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever, which causes migratory polyarthritis without dependent palpable purpura.
Incorrect: Ascending areflexic paralysis defines Guillain-Barré syndrome rather than Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

Correct: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is defined clinically by palpable purpura (predominantly buttocks/extensor legs) with normal platelets plus arthritis/arthralgia (knees/ankles), colicky abdominal pain (risk of intussusception), and IgA nephritis.
clinicalPearl: Classic HSP tetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks/lower legs, normal platelets) + large-joint arthralgia/arthritis + colicky abdominal pain (watch for ileo-ileal intussusception!) + haematuria/proteinuria (monitor BP and urine for 6–12 months).

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) presents with dependent palpable purpura, knee/ankle arthritis, colicky abdominal pain, and glomerulonephritis.

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with acute-onset facial asymmetry when asked to squeeze both eyes shut and smile, as shown in the photograph. Which localisation is correct, and what bedside assessments must be performed in every child with this presentation?
options: Left lower motor neurone facial palsy; check blood pressure and perform otoscopy
Right upper motor neurone facial palsy; perform immediate lumbar puncture and EEG
Left upper motor neurone facial palsy; order serum creatine kinase and muscle biopsy
Right lower motor neurone facial palsy; test visual fields and prescribe oral pyridostigmine
Bilateral congenital myasthenia; administer IV edrophonium and order chest CT
optionRationales: Correct: Inability to close the left eye alongside left mouth droop indicates a left LMN CN VII palsy (Bell's palsy); in children, always examine the tympanic membrane/mastoid (acute otitis media/mastoiditis) and measure blood pressure (severe hypertension from renal disease or coarctation can present with LMN facial palsy!).

Incorrect: Upper motor neurone lesions spare upper facial muscles (eye closure and forehead wrinkling) due to bilateral cortical innervation, and the weakness here affects the left eye and left mouth.
Incorrect: Failure to close the left eye confirms involvement of both upper and lower facial divisions on the left side, localising to an LMN facial nerve lesion rather than UMN.
Incorrect: The right eye closes tightly and the right corner of the mouth elevates normally; the paralysed side is the left side (viewer's right).
Incorrect: Acute unilateral paralysis sparing the right side of the face does not fit bilateral neuromuscular junction disease.
clinicalPearl: In any child with Bell's palsy (LMN CN VII), never forget two mandatory bedside checks: (1) Otoscopy (rule out acute otitis media/cholesteatoma/Ramsay Hunt vesicles) and (2) Blood pressure (renal/coarctation hypertension can cause LMN facial palsy!).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute unilateral inability to close the eye and retract the mouth indicates LMN CN VII palsy; check otoscopy and blood pressure in every paediatric case.

(13.2) Likely cause: Post-viral / idiopathic (HSV-1 reactivation); in children also check otitis media / mastoiditis, Varicella-zoster, EBV, and blood pressure (coarctation/renal HTN can present with LMN facial palsy in children!).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: During the critical phase of dengue haemorrhagic fever in a 9-year-old child, serial 3-hourly measurements using the capillary tube and reader shown demonstrate a rising reading from 37% to 46% alongside a falling platelet count and narrowing pulse pressure. What does this trend signify?
options: Entering the convalescent phase with reabsorption of pleural and ascitic fluid
Ongoing plasma leakage with worsening haemoconcentration requiring fluid escalation
Concealed gastrointestinal haemorrhage requiring immediate packed red blood cell transfusion
Normal physiological diurnal variation in infant erythrocyte mass
Acute haemolytic uraemic syndrome secondary to dengue viraemia
optionRationales: Incorrect: Reabsorption during the recovery phase causes haemodilution (a falling PCV) alongside rising blood pressure, widening pulse pressure, and brisk diuresis.

Correct: A progressive rise in Packed Cell Volume (PCV) with narrowing pulse pressure reflects worsening intravascular volume depletion from capillary plasma leakage, indicating need for IV fluid escalation (crystalloid bolus or colloid).
Incorrect: Concealed haemorrhage in dengue causes an unexpected drop (not a rise from 37% to 46%) in PCV despite persistent tachycardia or refractory shock.
Incorrect: A 9-percentage-point acute rise in PCV during active dengue leakage is pathological haemoconcentration, not diurnal variation.
Incorrect: Acute intravascular haemolysis lowers PCV/haemoglobin sharply rather than producing haemoconcentration.
clinicalPearl: Know both critical PCV trends in DHF: Rising PCV + shock = worsening plasma leakage (needs colloid/crystalloid bolus); Falling PCV + persistent shock = concealed haemorrhage (needs urgent cross-matched blood transfusion!).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Serial 3-hourly PCV monitoring identifies progressive haemoconcentration from plasma leakage (rising PCV) versus concealed bleeding (falling PCV in shock).

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: An 8-year-old boy is found to have eight flat, well-demarcated light-brown macules larger than 5 mm in diameter over his back as shown, together with bilateral axillary freckling. What are the most likely diagnosis and its mode of inheritance?
options: Tuberous sclerosis complex; X-linked recessive
McCune-Albright syndrome; autosomal recessive
Neurofibromatosis type 1; autosomal dominant
Sturge-Weber syndrome; autosomal dominant
Ataxia-telangiectasia; X-linked dominant
optionRationales: Incorrect: Tuberous sclerosis is autosomal dominant and classically causes hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, and shagreen patches rather than numerous café-au-lait spots.
Incorrect: McCune-Albright syndrome arises from post-zygotic somatic GNAS mutations (non-inherited) and features fewer, jagged 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait lesions without axillary freckling.

Correct: Six or more café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal) plus axillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe sign) meet diagnostic criteria for Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder.
Incorrect: Sturge-Weber syndrome is sporadic and manifests with a trigeminal port-wine stain (naevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angioma rather than hyperpigmented macules.
Incorrect: Ataxia-telangiectasia is autosomal recessive and presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia and oculocutaneous telangiectasias.
clinicalPearl: NF1 diagnostic threshold for café-au-lait macules: >=6 spots >5 mm in prepubertal children (or >15 mm postpubertal); screen for Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), optic pathway gliomas, hypertension, and scoliosis.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Multiple café-au-lait patches with axillary freckling are classic neurocutaneous stigmata of autosomal dominant Neurofibromatosis type 1.

domain: 4.6 PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY, DERMATOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with the unilateral eye finding shown in the photograph. If further examination demonstrates ipsilateral miosis and facial anhidrosis with full, unrestricted extraocular movements, which diagnosis best accounts for these findings?
options: Oculomotor (CN III) nerve palsy (midbrain lesion)
Congenital isolated levator palpebrae maldevelopment
Bell's palsy (peripheral CN VII facial neuropathy)
Horner syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain lesion)
Juvenile ocular myasthenia gravis (NMJ disorder)
optionRationales: Incorrect: CN III palsy produces severe complete ptosis alongside a dilated pupil (mydriasis) and an eye deviated 'down and out' due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action.
Incorrect: Simple congenital ptosis is an isolated myogenic levator defect and does not cause ipsilateral miosis or facial anhidrosis.
Incorrect: Facial nerve palsy weakens orbicularis oculi causing inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos) rather than upper eyelid ptosis and miosis.

Correct: Mild right upper eyelid ptosis (denervation of Müller's muscle) combined with ipsilateral miosis and anhidrosis with preserved extraocular motility defines Horner syndrome; in children, exclude thoracic/cervical neuroblastoma or surgical sympathetic injury.
Incorrect: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable, fluctuating ptosis and variable diplopia/ophthalmoplegia, never pupillary miosis or anhidrosis.
clinicalPearl: Distinguish ptosis causes by pupil & eye movements: Horner = mild ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis (check neck/chest for neuroblastoma!); CN III = severe ptosis + mydriasis + 'down-and-out' gaze; Myasthenia = fatigable ptosis + normal pupils.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Evaluate unilateral paediatric ptosis by checking pupil size and eye movements to distinguish Horner syndrome, CN III palsy, congenital ptosis, and myasthenia gravis.

domain: 4.7 IMMUNISATION, NOTIFIABLE DISEASES, NEEDLES, SAMPLING & EQUIPMENT (9 STATIONS)
stem: Referring to the colour-coded needle gauge chart shown, which needle gauge ranges are recommended for deep intramuscular (IM) versus subcutaneous (SC) paediatric injections?
options: 18G–19G (pink or light yellow) for deep IM; 21G–22G (green or black) for SC
26G–27G (brown or grey) for deep IM; 18G–20G (pink or yellow) for SC
24G–25G (purple or orange) for deep IM; 19G–20G (light yellow or yellow) for SC
18G–20G (pink or yellow) for deep IM; 22G–23G (black or blue) for SC
21G–23G (green or blue) for deep IM; 25G–27G (orange or brown) for SC
optionRationales: Incorrect: 18G–19G needles are wide-bore drawing-up or blood transfusion needles unsuitable for paediatric IM injections, and 21G–22G are too large for SC administration.
Incorrect: This reverses gauge sizing: 26G–27G needles are too short/fine for deep IM muscle penetration, while 18G–20G are excessively traumatic for subcutaneous tissue.
Incorrect: 19G–20G needles are inappropriate for subcutaneous injections, and 24G is primarily a fine/neonatal gauge rather than standard deep IM.
Incorrect: 18G–20G needles cause unnecessary muscle trauma in children, and 22G–23G needles are IM rather than SC gauges.

Correct: Deep IM injections require sturdier 21G–23G needles (21G dark green, 22G black, or 23G dark blue) to penetrate muscle safely, whereas SC injections use finer, shorter 25G–27G needles (25G orange, 26G brown, or 27G grey).
clinicalPearl: ISO colour-coding to memorise for OSCEs: Deep IM = 21G Green / 22G Black / 23G Blue (23G–25G 25 mm for infant vaccines); Subcutaneous = 25G Orange / 26G Brown / 27G Grey.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Guide for Paediatric Vaccines & Sri Lankan EPI Schedule
guideCitation.keyPoint: Correct needle selection matches route and tissue depth: 21G–23G for deep IM injections and 25G–27G for subcutaneous injections.

domain: 4.7 IMMUNISATION, NOTIFIABLE DISEASES, NEEDLES, SAMPLING & EQUIPMENT (9 STATIONS)
stem: Regarding the Sri Lankan communicable disease notification form (Health 544) shown, which diseases belong to Group A requiring immediate notification upon clinical suspicion, and to whom should the attending doctor send the form?
options: Cholera, plague, and yellow fever; sent by the attending medical officer to the local MOH
Dengue fever, enteric fever, and leptospirosis; sent by the ward nurse after PCR confirmation to the WHO
Measles, mumps, and chickenpox; sent by the hospital pharmacist to the Regional Director of Health Services
Tuberculosis, leprosy, and malaria; sent only after hospital discharge to the Epidemiology Unit
Pertussis, diphtheria, and hepatitis A; handed to the parents to deliver to the Public Health Inspector
optionRationales: Correct: Under Sri Lankan surveillance, Group A diseases (cholera, plague, yellow fever) require immediate notification by telephone/special message on suspicion—without waiting for lab confirmation—with Form Health 544 filled by the attending medical officer and sent to the local Medical Officer of Health (MOH).

Incorrect: Dengue, typhoid, and leptospirosis belong to Group B (notified promptly via Health 544 on suspicion), and the attending medical officer—not only after lab confirmation—notifies the local MOH.
Incorrect: Measles is Group B and varicella is not Group A; notification is the statutory duty of the attending medical officer to the local MOH.
Incorrect: Delaying notification until discharge undermines outbreak containment and contact tracing; Health 544 must be initiated immediately upon clinical suspicion.

Incorrect: Health 544 is transmitted through official health channels to the local MOH (who coordinates PHI field investigation), never left to parents, and those diseases are Group B rather than Group A.
clinicalPearl: Never wait for laboratory confirmation to fill Form Health 544! Notify on clinical suspicion: Group A (Cholera, Plague, Yellow Fever) = immediate phone call + Health 544 to the patient's Medical Officer of Health (MOH).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Group A notifiable diseases (cholera, plague, yellow fever) require immediate reporting on suspicion via Health 544 by the attending medical officer to the patient's MOH.

domain: 4.7 IMMUNISATION, NOTIFIABLE DISEASES, NEEDLES, SAMPLING & EQUIPMENT (9 STATIONS)
stem: For the two paediatric procedures listed in the image—(a) intramuscular pentavalent vaccine in a 3-year-old child and (b) subcutaneous soluble insulin in a 10-year-old boy—which pair of labelled needles (A–F) is most appropriate?
options: Needle E (fine clear-pink hub) for IM pentavalent and Needle D (blue hub) for SC insulin
Needle D (blue hub) for IM pentavalent and Needle E (fine clear-pink hub) for SC insulin
Needle A (long orange hub) for IM pentavalent and Needle F (green hub) for SC insulin
Needle F (green hub) for IM pentavalent and Needle B (purple hub) for SC insulin
Needle B (purple hub) for IM pentavalent and Needle A (long orange hub) for SC insulin
optionRationales: Incorrect: Reversing these risks superficial adipose deposition of the aluminium-adjuvanted pentavalent vaccine (causing sterile nodules/poor immunogenicity) and inadvertent intramuscular insulin injection (causing rapid hypoglycaemia).

Correct: A 23G blue-hub needle (D) is standard for deep IM vaccines and IM anaphylaxis adrenaline in young children, while the fine short needle (E, 26G–27G range) is appropriate for subcutaneous soluble insulin.

Incorrect: Needle A is a long drawing-up/spinal-length needle unsuitable for a 3-year-old's thigh muscle, risking periosteal or neurovascular injury, and a 21G green needle (F) is too wide and long for subcutaneous insulin.

Incorrect: 21G green (F) is unnecessarily wide for routine paediatric vaccination when 23G blue (D) is available, and purple (B, 18G/24G) is suboptimal compared with dedicated fine SC insulin needles.
Incorrect: Neither needle matches safe tissue depth for these paediatric IM and SC procedures.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan OSCEs, 23G Blue (needle D) is your go-to answer for both paediatric IM vaccines (pentavalent) and IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis; use fine short needles (E, 26G–27G) for SC insulin.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Guide for Paediatric Vaccines & Sri Lankan EPI Schedule
guideCitation.keyPoint: Select 23G blue (needle D) for paediatric IM pentavalent or IM adrenaline and fine short needles (E, 26G–27G) for subcutaneous insulin.

domain: 4.7 IMMUNISATION, NOTIFIABLE DISEASES, NEEDLES, SAMPLING & EQUIPMENT (9 STATIONS)
stem: From the labelled paediatric instruments shown (A1–A2, B1–B4, C1–C3), which selection correctly matches (1) inspecting watery ear discharge in a 2-month-old baby and (2) delivering controlled IV maintenance fluids to a newborn without risking fluid overload?
options: A2 (metal probe) for the ear; B1 (30G needle) with C1 (standard adult giving set) for newborn IV fluids
A1 (otoscope) for the ear; B2 (27G needle) with C2 (standard Y-port fluid set) for newborn IV fluids
A1 (otoscope) for the ear; B4 (scalp-vein needle) with C3 (micro-drip burette set) for newborn IV fluids
A2 (metal probe) for the ear; B4 (scalp-vein needle) with C1 (standard adult giving set) for newborn IV fluids
B3 (23G needle) for the ear; A1 (otoscope) with C3 (micro-drip burette set) for newborn IV fluids
optionRationales: Incorrect: Inserting a rigid probe blindly into an infant ear canal risks tympanic perforation, and connecting an unmeasured adult giving set (15–20 drops/mL) to a newborn risks fatal volume overload.
Incorrect: A bare 27G hypodermic needle cannot maintain secure venous access, and a standard macro-drip tubing without a burette chamber lacks neonatal volume-limiting safeguards.

Correct: An otoscope (A1) with a small paediatric speculum inspects the infant's tympanic membrane, while a neonatal cannula or winged butterfly scalp-vein needle (B4) attached to a graduated micro-drip burette set (C3, 60 drops/mL) prevents accidental neonatal fluid overload.
Incorrect: Neither the metal probe for ear examination nor an un-buretted adult giving set for newborn maintenance fluids is safe.
Incorrect: An otoscope (A1) is not a vascular access tool, and a 23G needle is not used to inspect ear discharge.
clinicalPearl: Always pair neonatal IV infusions with a paediatric micro-drip burette chamber (60 drops/mL, C3) and a 24G yellow cannula or butterfly needle (B4) to prevent catastrophic iatrogenic fluid overload.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Use an otoscope for infant ear assessment, and use a small-gauge neonatal cannula/butterfly needle with a 60 drops/mL burette set for controlled newborn IV fluid therapy.
